title: Topic picker, round 2
subtitle: Only new topics, none from round 1. Hooks are from memory, fact-checked only once picked. Already picked: 31 (11 from the plan page, 20 from round 1). You can still select any text and press C to comment.

items.title: Why we hiccup
items.note: A leftover from our water-breathing ancestors? The theories, and what actually stops one.

items.title: Why some people sneeze in sunlight
items.note: The photic sneeze reflex: about 1 in 4 people; crossed wires near the eye nerve.

items.title: Why your ears pop on a plane
items.note: A tiny tube balancing pressure; why yawning and chewing help.

items.title: Why cracking knuckles pops
items.note: A gas bubble forming (filmed in an MRI, 2015); a doctor cracked one hand for 60 years to test arthritis.

items.title: 11 days without sleep
items.note: Randy Gardner, 1964: what happened to his brain, and why the record is no longer tracked.

items.title: Why helium makes your voice squeaky
items.note: It does not change your vocal cords, only how sound travels; a heavy gas does the opposite.

items.title: Why babies can breathe and swallow at once
items.note: Their larynx sits high; ours dropped, which let us speak and made us choke.

items.title: Astronauts grow taller in space
items.note: Up to about 5 cm, and lose it back on Earth.

items.title: The Moon is drifting away, 3.8 cm a year
items.note: Measured with mirrors Apollo astronauts left there.

items.title: How we know what stars are made of
items.note: A philosopher said we never could (1835); spectra proved him wrong decades later.

items.title: Voyager 1: the farthest thing we ever made
items.note: And the golden record with music and greetings aboard.

items.title: Why shooting stars peak in August
items.note: Earth crossing a comet's dust trail every year.

items.title: Time runs slower on the ground floor
items.note: Clocks at different heights tick differently; measured with atomic clocks 33 cm apart.

items.title: Why a steel ship floats
items.note: It is mostly air: displacement explained with a cup of water.

items.title: Why a kettle is loudest before it boils
items.note: Bubbles collapsing at the start; the roar calms once the water is hot throughout.

items.title: Why soap bubbles have colours
items.note: Thin-film interference: the film is thinner than light's wavelength.

items.title: Why bubbles are round
items.note: The smallest surface for a given air: soap is lazy.

items.title: Why a spoon looks broken in a glass
items.note: Refraction, and why fish are not where they look.

items.title: Why toast lands butter side down
items.note: Not bad luck: table height gives it half a turn (a 1995 paper).

items.title: How Shazam recognises a song in a noisy bar
items.note: Audio fingerprints: peaks in a sound map.

items.title: How your phone knows your fingerprint
items.note: Ridges as a tiny capacitor map, or light, or sound.

items.title: Why Wi-Fi weakens through walls
items.note: 2.4 vs 5 GHz, water in walls and in people.

items.title: How sites store your password without knowing it
items.note: Hashing; why '123456' falls in a second.

items.title: How an electric car charges itself while braking
items.note: The motor run backwards as a generator.

items.title: How a photo becomes JPEG
items.note: Throwing away what the eye will not miss.

items.title: The year 2038 problem
items.note: A counter of seconds since 1970 runs out: the next Y2K.

items.title: The dress: blue-black or white-gold?
items.note: Why brains disagreed in 2015: assumptions about the light.

items.title: Why we see faces in sockets and clouds
items.note: Pareidolia: a face detector tuned to never miss one.

items.title: Why wheels spin backwards on video
items.note: The camera samples too slowly (the wagon-wheel effect).

items.title: Seeing changes what you hear
items.note: The McGurk effect: the lips win.

items.title: Two squares of the same grey
items.note: The checker-shadow illusion: the brain corrects for shadows.

items.title: Why the Moon follows your car
items.note: Very far things barely shift when you move.

items.title: Phantom phone vibrations
items.note: Most phone users feel buzzes that never happened.

items.title: How Hebrew came back from the dead
items.note: A written-only language became a mother tongue again within decades.

items.title: Why 'huh?' is the same in every language
items.note: A 2013 study across 31 languages.

items.title: Why tongue twisters twist
items.note: The brain plans sounds ahead and the plans collide.

items.title: Do children really learn languages faster?
items.note: What the critical-period research shows, and where adults win.

items.title: Why 'w' is called 'double u'
items.note: It was written as two u's (or v's).

items.title: Why whistled languages exist
items.note: Whole languages whistled across valleys (Canary Islands, Turkey).

items.title: How a groove on vinyl holds a song
items.note: The needle traces the sound wave itself.

items.title: Is a Stradivarius really better?
items.note: Blind tests: top soloists could not tell, and often preferred new violins.

items.title: Why 'Happy Birthday' was copyrighted until 2016
items.note: A song everyone sang, owned by a company, until a court case.

items.title: Why the duduk sounds sad
items.note: Its double reed and apricot wood; UNESCO's list (local).

items.title: Why old paintings crack
items.note: Craquelure: and how experts use it to catch forgeries.

items.title: Why screens and printers mix colours differently
items.note: Light adds (RGB), ink subtracts (CMYK).

items.title: Why bees build hexagons
items.note: The least wax for the most honey; proved only in 1999.

items.title: The seven bridges of Königsberg
items.note: A Sunday-walk puzzle that started graph theory (Euler, 1736).

items.title: Why folding a pizza slice keeps it stiff
items.note: Gauss's theorem again: bend one way and it cannot bend the other.

items.title: 7 shuffles make a deck random
items.note: Fewer is not enough; more barely helps (Bayer and Diaconis, 1992).

items.title: The golden ratio is overrated
items.note: Most 'it's everywhere' claims do not survive measuring.

items.title: How a computer makes a random number
items.note: Pseudo-random formulas, and lava lamps at Cloudflare.

items.title: Why birds on power lines don't get shocked
items.note: No path to the ground; one foot on another wire would be the end.

items.title: Why home electricity is AC
items.note: Edison vs Tesla and Westinghouse, and the transformer.

items.title: How a solar panel makes electricity
items.note: Light knocking electrons loose in silicon.

items.title: Lightning is hotter than the Sun's surface
items.note: About 5 times hotter, for a few microseconds.

items.title: Why you get static shocks in winter
items.note: Dry air lets charge build up.

items.title: Why your charger gets warm
items.note: No conversion is perfect: where the lost energy goes.

items.title: Why rain smells
items.note: Petrichor: a molecule from soil bacteria we can smell at tiny amounts.

items.title: Why forecasts stop at about 10 days
items.note: Chaos: the butterfly effect started with a rounded number (Lorenz).

items.title: Why clouds float though they weigh tonnes
items.note: Tiny droplets spread over a huge volume of rising air.

items.title: Are no two snowflakes alike?
items.note: Probably true for big ones, and why a lab made twins.

items.title: Why Yerevan has hot summers and cold winters
items.note: Far from any sea, on a high plateau (local).

items.title: Why thunder rumbles
items.note: One crack heard from different distances along the bolt.

items.title: Why pencils are hexagonal
items.note: They do not roll off the desk, and fit the grip.

items.title: Why most zips say YKK
items.note: One Japanese company makes about half of the world's zips.

items.title: Why jeans have a tiny pocket
items.note: It was for a pocket watch.

items.title: Why shoelaces come untied
items.note: A 2017 slow-motion study: stomping loosens, swinging pulls.

items.title: Why bottle caps have 21 teeth
items.note: The 1892 crown cap and the number that sealed best.

items.title: Why the power symbol is a 1 and a 0
items.note: On and off from binary, merged into one sign.

items.title: Traffic jams from nowhere
items.note: A 2008 experiment: cars on a circle, no obstacle, a jam forms anyway.

items.title: Why rail gauges differ
items.note: 1435 mm in Europe, 1520 mm in the former USSR including Armenia.

items.title: Why planes leave white trails
items.note: Contrails: water vapour freezing; why some stay and some don't.

items.title: Why a moving bicycle stays upright
items.note: Not only gyroscopes: researchers built a bike that disproves the textbook answer.

items.title: Why most countries drive on the right
items.note: Horses, swords, Napoleon and Britain: myth vs evidence.

items.title: The Wings of Tatev
items.note: Once the world's longest reversible cable car; how it holds (local).

items.title: Roman concrete heals itself
items.note: Lime lumps that seal cracks with water (2023 study).

items.title: The Antikythera mechanism
items.note: A 2,000-year-old gear computer for the sky.

items.title: Ice in the desert: Persian ice houses
items.note: Yakhchals made and kept ice through summer.

items.title: The pyramid builders were not slaves
items.note: Workers' villages, bread and beer rations, and their graves.

items.title: Garni temple, taken apart and put back
items.note: Fell in 1679, rebuilt stone by stone in the 1970s (local).

items.title: A light bulb burning since 1901
items.note: The Livermore fire station bulb, and the cartel that limited bulb life.

items.title: Why CAPTCHAs ask for traffic lights
items.note: You are labelling data for self-driving cars.

items.title: Why incognito mode doesn't hide you
items.note: It only forgets locally.

items.title: Why emoji look different on every phone
items.note: The code is shared, the drawing is not.

items.title: How streaming picks your video quality
items.note: Chunks and adaptive bitrate, second by second.

items.title: How a recommendation feed decides
items.note: What you watched trains what you see next.

items.title: Why diamonds are expensive
items.note: Not rare: a marketing campaign ('A diamond is forever', 1947).

items.title: The last digit of your card checks the others
items.note: The Luhn algorithm catches typos.

items.title: Banks create money when they lend
items.note: How a loan makes new money appear.

items.title: Why plane tickets change price
items.note: Dynamic pricing and the myth of cookies raising prices.

items.title: Why the apricot's Latin name is 'Armenian plum'
items.note: Prunus armeniaca: how the name travelled.

items.title: Why Yerevan is pink
items.note: Volcanic tuff from Aragats: light, soft to cut, hard to break.

items.title: Byurakan and Ambartsumian
items.note: The observatory that found where stars are born (local science).

items.title: Did Stalin send Churchill Armenian brandy?
items.note: A favourite story checked against the evidence.

items.title: Sevan's ishkhan trout
items.note: The lake's own fish, and why it nearly disappeared.

items.title: The oldest map of the world with Armenia on it
items.note: The Babylonian world map (Imago Mundi) names Urartu.
